description:
We are Azharelly, Omar, Meryem, Dory and Sofia

Our interests range from arts to computer science, and from human health to space exploration. For the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge we brought them together to build VitalisX, an offline crew health co-pilot for deep-space missions that answers the challenge "Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions"

We combined our different skills, helped each other with our different difficulties, and, most importantly, learned with one another
summary: VitalisX is an offline-first health co-pilot for astronaut crews on long missions. On a trip to Mars, Earth can be up to 22 minutes away, so astronauts must notice changes in their own health. Instead of using Earth population averages, which can mislead in space, VitalisX learns each astronaut's own normal from a short daily check-in and flags changes as Watch or Alert. Each alert comes with one clear action and a "Why am I seeing this?" screen that shows the evidence and the rule behind it. It also tracks radiation dose against NASA's 600 mSv career limit, shows live NASA DONKI space-weather events as context, and prepares a structured SBAR report for the flight surgeon, queued with the Earth communication delay. Built as an installable web app that works without internet, VitalisX uses simulated crew data and is decision support, not diagnosis. The same approach could support remote medicine on Earth, such as Antarctic stations and ships.
details:
VITALISX

Introduction

We are Azharelly Cervantes, Mohammad Omar Ghani, Meryem Elkhattabi, Dory Saint-Surin and Sofia Moita, from Mexico, Pakistan, Morocco, Canada and Portugal, and we hope to give you a detailed description of our project, VitalisX.

How did we come up with this? You must be wondering… Well, we're a group of people with a wide scope of interests, from arts to computer science, from human health to space exploration, and much more. All our interests converged into this one idea, this one "baby" of ours, managing to gather our different skills, understanding our different difficulties, and most importantly, learning with one another.

So, with no further delay, we are happy and thrilled to show you our project.

1. What exactly does it do?

VitalisX is an offline-first crew health co-pilot designed for deep-space exploration, but suitable for Earth exploration scenarios, or other health monitoring needs. Instead of comparing astronauts' health markers with Earth population averages, which can fail in space due to physiological adaptations, VitalisX learns each astronaut's in-flight baseline. See Table I for the differences in health markers between Earth and deep space.

Table I: credits, Sofia Moita

The app monitors key health markers (such as glucose, core temperature, bone and muscle, etc.), flags changes from each person's own normal early, and advises one "Next Best Action" with full mathematical explainability ("Why am I seeing this?"). It also generates delay-aware SBAR clinical reports for flight surgeons on Earth. All of this through a calm interactive interface that features a clickable anatomical body map.

It operates with two states: Watch and Alert. Our software lets each astronaut keep an eye on their vitals and alerts them to unusual data. Based on NASA-conducted research, astronauts' vitals tend to differ from their values on Earth (see Table I). VitalisX provides continuous, context-aware tracking across key health metrics to deliver tailored advice for each one:

  • Glycemia (Blood Glucose): Monitored with contextual timing (fasting, pre-meal, post-meal), so that each reading is compared only with readings taken in the same context.
  • Fever & Core Body Temperature: Tracks temperature alongside context (resting, post-exercise, post-meal), so that readings after exercise are not compared with resting ones.
  • Blood Pressure & Hemodynamics: Monitors blood pressure against the astronaut's own baseline, which already reflects the fluid shift toward the head in microgravity.
  • Vision & Neuro-Ocular Stats (SANS): A daily self-check of vision (for example, blurred focus) to flag possible changes early. It is not a diagnosis.
  • Bones & Muscles: Logs exercise adherence to help the crew keep up their bone and muscle routine.
  • Sleeping Habits: Tracks sleep duration and quality from the daily check-in to help notice circadian disruption and fatigue.
  • Radiation Exposure Budgeting: Tracks cumulative radiation dose against NASA's 600 mSv career limit and shows real space-weather events from NASA DONKI.

2. How does it work?

A touch-friendly interface lets astronauts log vitals, sleep and symptoms quickly. For further details, the user can open "Why am I seeing this?", where every alert shows a trend chart of the last 7 readings against the person's usual range, the exact rule that fired, a 3-step action ladder and the sources.

Personalized in-flight baselines: VitalisX computes a 28-day personal baseline for each astronaut (our own design rule). Deviations are evaluated with a robust z-score based on the median and the Median Absolute Deviation (MAD), so one unusual reading does not distort the person's normal. A WATCH state is raised for sustained deviations, and an ALERT for strong deviations or readings outside absolute limits.

  • Explainability and daily check-in: astronauts do a daily check-in (for example, sleep duration), which recomputes their health status. Every alert has a "Why am I seeing this?" button that shows a chart of the last 7 readings against the astronaut's personal range, the exact rule that fired and the linked scientific references.
  • Comprehensive domain coverage:

A. Radiation Exposure: Checks cumulative exposure against the universal 600 mSv limit defined in NASA-STD-3001. It projects the dose at arrival (using Mars transit rates) and shows live solar flare, coronal mass ejection, geomagnetic storm and Solar Energetic Particle data from the NASA DONKI API as context. These events are not converted into a dose.

B. Ocular Health (SANS): A self-check on vision changes, such as blurred focus. It can flag possible changes early; it is not a diagnosis.

C. Sleep and Behavioral Health: Checks sleep duration and quality with the daily check-in.

D. Bone, Muscle and Metabolism: Checks weekly exercise adherence.

  • Offline-first and delay-aware SBAR outbox: The app is built to operate across 3–22 minute one-way Mars communication delays and signal blackouts. It works offline after the first load, the data stays on the device, and space-weather data is read live when online. An always-visible Emergency button opens a guided flow with a full summary of the person for acute care.

3. What are the benefits?

  • Earth-independent medical autonomy: the crew can notice subtle health changes early without waiting up to 44 minutes for a reply.
  • Fewer false alarms: each reading is compared with the person's own normal using the median and MAD, so one unusual value does not distort the baseline.
  • Transparent and honest decision support: every alert shows statistical evidence, a cited source or the label "our own design rule", and a step-by-step suggestion.

4. What do we hope to achieve?

We still hope to make some improvements. For example, we'd like to test the app with real mission scenarios, connect it to real wearable and medical data, and add a way for each astronaut to choose what is shared with the crew and with Earth.

We made this prototype in the hope of helping not only crews that go into deep-space missions, but also in "closer" situations on Earth. This, we hope, will help crews notice health problems earlier on a long mission. Beyond space exploration (such as Artemis), VitalisX's offline-first architecture, personal-baseline engine and structured SBAR handover could be adapted to remote telemedicine on Earth, supporting Antarctic research stations and maritime crews, among others.

5. How creative is this project?

We designed our site to be interactive, simple, and objective for fast and easy use. We kept the app to a small set of focused screens, so astronauts can reach everything in a tap or two, with a dark theme that is gentle on the eyes. Our system prioritizes proactive vitals management and offers tailored self-care suggestions rather than giving medical diagnoses, keeping the crew in full control of their health. Finally, our app uses a local database that stores a complete copy of the data on the device, so the app keeps working without a connection.

6. What factors did your team consider?

When designing our project, we focused on three main factors: space health risks, quick and easy use, and data safety. To keep the app simple, we built a small set of screens with a body map of custom drawings by our teammate, large touch targets and a gentle dark mode. Technically, the app works offline after the first load using a local database, and it checks every entry to prevent mistakes. Finally, we prioritized crew autonomy by offering tailored self-care suggestions rather than medical diagnoses.

7. What tools did we use?

  • Languages: TypeScript (application, statistical detection engine, and simulated data generator) and JavaScript (verification and check scripts).
  • Frontend & offline storage: React, Vite, Progressive Web App (PWA) with Service Worker precaching, and IndexedDB managed via Dexie.js (7 local object stores), deployed on Vercel.
  • NASA data & scientific standards: NASA DONKI API (space weather), NASA-STD-3001 Vol. 1 (V1 4030 and V1 4031) and Vol. 2 (V2 6003), MSL RAD Mars cruise telemetry (Zeitlin et al., 2013), and published peer-reviewed spaceflight literature (Barger et al., 2014; Battelino et al., 2019; Gew et al., 2026; Guo et al., 2015; Lang et al., 2004; Norsk et al., 2015; Otsuka et al., 2021; Stahn et al., 2017).
